blocks.text: INT8 quantization represents model weights using 8-bit integers, 256 distinct possible values, a widely used, well supported precision level that strikes a practical balance between the aggressive memory savings of 4-bit quantization, covered in the earlier LoRA and QLoRA module, and the higher precision of full floating point representation.

This topic covers INT8 specifically as a deployment focused quantization format, distinct from the training focused 4-bit quantization covered earlier, setting up a direct comparison in the next topic with INT4.
1. What INT8 Quantization Means
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472248855-489105654.png

INT8 quantization converts each floating point weight value into an 8-bit integer, one of 256 possible discrete values, a mapping that requires far less memory than full floating point precision while retaining considerably more precision than the 4-bit formats covered earlier in this course.
2. Mapping Floating Point Values to Integers

blocks.alt: Mapping Floating Point Values to Integers
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472248856-365254617.png

Converting a continuous range of floating point values into 256 discrete integer levels requires a scale factor, determining exactly how the real number range maps onto the available integer levels, the same fundamental idea as the scaling factors covered throughout the earlier LoRA and QLoRA module.
3. INT8 Memory and Speed Benefits
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472248856-683696337.png

INT8 delivers a fourfold memory reduction compared to full FP32 precision, and many inference platforms include dedicated hardware acceleration for INT8 computation, delivering meaningful speed improvements alongside the memory savings, similar in spirit to the FP16 and BF16 hardware acceleration covered in the Training Infrastructure module.
4. INT8 vs the 4-Bit Quantization Covered Earlier

blocks.alt: INT8 vs the 4-Bit Quantization Covered Earlier
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472248857-290105429.png

Compared to the NF4 format covered in the earlier LoRA and QLoRA module, INT8 offers considerably more representable levels, 256 versus 16, trading away some of NF4 more aggressive memory savings for meaningfully higher numeric precision, a reasonable choice when the extra precision matters more than squeezing out the absolute maximum memory reduction.
5. Calibrating an INT8 Quantization Scheme
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472248857-44599167.png

Choosing an effective scale factor for INT8 quantization typically involves calibration, covered generally in the earlier What Is Quantization topic, running representative data through the model to observe the actual range of weight and activation values that need to be represented well within the available 256 levels.
6. INT8 and Inference Hardware Support
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472248858-20278247.png

INT8 enjoys particularly broad hardware support across a wide range of inference platforms, from data center accelerators down to some edge devices, making it one of the more portable and widely deployable quantization formats covered in this module.

blocks.title: This portability makes INT8 a common deployment default
blocks.content: Given its broad hardware support and reasonable precision, INT8 is frequently the default quantization choice for deploying a fine-tuned model, covered further in the Inference and Serving module later in this course.

blocks.text: 7. Quality Impact of INT8 Quantization
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472249185-644080480.png

Because INT8 retains considerably more precision than 4-bit formats, its quality impact on a deployed model is generally modest, often difficult to distinguish from the full precision original for many practical tasks, making it an attractive default when some memory savings are wanted without a significant quality tradeoff.
8. INT8 for Fine-Tuned Model Deployment

After completing a fine-tuning process using any of the techniques covered throughout this course, quantizing the resulting model to INT8 for deployment is a common practical step, reducing the deployed model memory footprint and often improving inference speed without a training run of its own.
9. When INT8 Is the Right Choice

INT8 is the right choice when broad hardware compatibility and a reliable, well understood quality versus efficiency tradeoff matter more than achieving the most aggressive possible memory reduction, which more specialized techniques like GPTQ or AWQ, covered later in this module, aim for at 4-bit precision instead.
Worked Example

A team finishes fine-tuning a model and wants to deploy it broadly across a mix of inference hardware, some of which does not support more exotic 4-bit quantization formats. Choosing INT8 quantization for their deployment gives them broad compatibility and a fourfold memory reduction from full precision, with quality impact minimal enough not to concern their evaluation team.

For a separate, more memory constrained deployment target later, they revisit the more aggressive 4-bit techniques covered elsewhere in this module, recognizing that INT8 was the right default for their initial broad deployment but not necessarily for every future scenario.
Common Mistakes

items: Assuming INT8 and the 4-bit formats covered earlier in this course offer the same memory savings, when INT8 is meaningfully less aggressive
Skipping calibration and using a naive, poorly chosen scale factor that unnecessarily hurts quality
Not checking hardware support for INT8 acceleration before assuming a deployment target will benefit from it
Reaching for more aggressive 4-bit quantization by default when INT8 broad compatibility and reliable quality would have been more appropriate

blocks.text: Practice

For a model size you choose, calculate the memory footprint at INT8 precision compared to full FP32 precision, confirming the fourfold reduction, and compare that against the even smaller footprint 4-bit quantization, covered earlier in this course, would achieve for the same model.
Key Takeaway

INT8 quantization represents weights using 8-bit integers, 256 possible levels, delivering a fourfold memory reduction from full precision with broad hardware support and generally modest quality impact, making it a reliable, widely compatible default for deploying a fine-tuned model, positioned between the more aggressive 4-bit formats and full floating point precision on the efficiency versus quality spectrum.
